key_insight: Finite-shot quantum measurements make gradient-based attacks on variational quantum classifiers expensive, with attacker measurement cost growing superlinearly in input dimension instead of staying cheap as in classical backpropagation.
engineering_relevance: For quantum ML systems, shot-noise can act as an intrinsic defense, but only if the model is hard to classically simulate and the attacker must estimate gradients from repeated circuit executions.
method: Analyzed unbiased gradient-estimation attacks under finite measurement statistics.
Derived lower bounds on the measurement budget for single-step and iterative attacks, including scaling with dimension and norm concentration.
Compared quantum attack cost against a classical autodiff baseline and validated the scaling in simulation and on IBM hardware.
evidence_signal: Simulations up to 784 input dimensions and experiments on ibm_boston (4-qubit circuits, d=12) matched the predicted scaling laws, with device attacks tracking the ideal within a few percent at matched budgets.
watch_item: The defense depends on specific assumptions about gradient estimation and on the forward map being classically hard to simulate, so it may weaken if an attacker can exploit alternative access or lower-noise estimation strategies.
paper_title: When cheap gradients fail: the measurement cost of attacking quantum classifiers
